articles.title: A Roadmap for MEG Foundation Models
articles.summary: The article outlines a roadmap for developing foundation models for magnetoencephalography (MEG), a brain-signal modality valued for millisecond-level temporal resolution and stronger spatial interpretability than EEG. It argues the field is still early, with limited MEG-specific models, modest pretraining datasets, and immature benchmarks, and highlights key technical choices such as tokenization, sensor versus source representations, architectures, self-supervised objectives, and multimodal integration.
articles.advisor_relevance: This is an early research signal rather than a near-term commercial development. It points to potential future AI opportunities in neuroscience, clinical brain-function analysis, and multimodal biomedical data platforms, but the lack of named companies, deployment evidence, or financing details limits immediate investment relevance.

articles.title: H Company Releases NeoMME: A Family of 260M and 800M Single-Tower Multimodal Encoders That Drop the Vision Tower and Causal Decoder
articles.summary: H Company released NeoMME, a family of 260M and 800M bidirectional multimodal encoders that combine multilingual text tokens and raw image patches in a single Transformer, eliminating the need for a separate vision tower or causal decoder. The article highlights technical results including 0.523 nDCG@10 on ViDoRe v3 for the 260M model, 255x index compression, and 51.3 pages-per-second indexing throughput on one L40S, while noting acknowledged gaps in text retrieval.
articles.advisor_relevance: NeoMME points to continued progress in making multimodal retrieval more efficient, which could matter for enterprise AI search, document intelligence, and knowledge-management workflows where indexing cost and throughput are practical bottlenecks. However, the article is primarily a technical model release with limited commercial detail, so investment relevance is indirect and tied to broader efficiency gains in AI infrastructure and enterprise adoption.

articles.title: Meta FAIR Introduces AI Research Preference Models (RPMs): Ranking ML Experiments Before Spending GPU Hours
articles.summary: Meta FAIR, Oxford and UCL introduced AI Research Preference Models, or RPMs, which use frozen LLM judges to rank 15 proposed machine learning experiments before selecting one to execute. In AIRS-Bench testing, the approach improved the average normalized score from 0.684 to 0.729 and achieved the baseline 24-hour result in roughly 15 hours.
articles.advisor_relevance: This highlights a practical way AI labs may reduce wasted GPU cycles by ranking experiments before execution, which is relevant as compute availability and cost remain key bottlenecks in AI development. While still research-oriented, the work points to improving productivity in AI R&D and potentially lowering the capital intensity of model experimentation over time.
